But the question that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was -- that should have been asked was: Do you know the reasons for which, et cetera, and then if the answer was yes, you can go ahead and ask. But Ms. Susan Somers is quite right in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: I hope that his motives will emerge very soon and all the reasons for his testimony. I apologise to the Trial Chamber, but my reaction was because he put forward ten gross lies, and I wanted to look him in the eyes, to see whether he would still carry on drinking water as he did while he was sitting here.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like Mr. Kvocka to be shown a document now, please. The suggestion made was that I tender the documents later on, but I'd like to show a certificate of the iron ore mine of Ljubija, Prijedor, to have the witness shown this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Would the witness please take a look at the document and please don't say anything, for protective measures, before I ask you my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, would you hand a copy to Ms. Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Mr. Simic. What is the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a copy of the document? Can the Judges be provided with a copy, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, do you have before you a portion of the personal dossier and file of an individual, the particulars from the file of an individual?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that from the heading, from the signature and stamp, from everything, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Does it state that the individual to which this certificate refers to was employed from the 1st of January, 1980 to the 30th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it states.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: In the system that we had, could one person work at two work posts?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. That was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kvocka, I should like now to go back to your second visit to the locality. And Mrs. Kvocka did not testify about that because she wasn't there, so we're not in collusion there. The second time you went, who was there? Tell us all the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: There was Ckalja, himself, and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: How long did the search last?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: It lasted for quite a long time, but we didn't go early. We went at around noon or just after noon and went until it became dark, which means 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. And as I've already said, I think that second time we found the glass jar straight away, the half kilo glass jar. It wasn't a plastic container of two litres as the gentleman said, but we found this glass jar straight away because he knew where it was. He had received information, and then he sent us off to dig in this other place where he claimed there was 6.000 marks buried. However, we weren't able to find that other portion after having dug for five hours. The jar we found after two minutes of digging, but we weren't able to find the other things at all. So we didn't find any money at all. We couldn't find any money, although, according to the information that his sister conveyed to him, as he explained to us, that is, he took us to the exact location of where this was supposed to be, but there was no money there. And we dug around. He did most of the digging, but we helped him, and we dug in a circumference around that locality and found nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: The jar you mention, how was it closed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think it was the normal type of top to this particular type of jar. Then there was a piece of nylon with a rubber band.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, was there any water in the jar when you dug it up?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember. I didn't look very closely, but I think there was some drops of water. Whether it was just moisture or whether it was actually water, I can't say, but it did seem to be a bit of -- a bit moist, damp.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was the jar opened in front you, before your eyes at all?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Where did you part from Mr. Gruban and his friend?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Gruban and him went off together in between our two buildings, and I went to return the car back to my kum, Mr. Oklopcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from Ckalja later on how the two of them parted? Did Ckalja see what was in the jar? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: He said and he told us, so I can't actually say, but story was -- his story was after everything had been completed, from what Ckalja had said and what his friend had said, there was a small gold chain, several costume jewelry rings, and a watch which he said was a memento and was worthless, that it was an old watch, a gold-plated watch, but worthless. So that was as a memento. And he said he needed money to go and treat -- to pay for the treatment of his mother. That's what he said the first time, or Ckalja said what he said. So that was the reason that made me decide to go and help them in the first place, because all the other help and assistance was not that kind of assistance. So that was the reason. So although on the one hand it was an act -- an unpleasant thing to do, on the other hand, it did help.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you mentioned a watch and you talked about a memento. To whom was it a memento?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: He said that it was his sister's remembrance of her husband, I think. I think that's what was said. But it was a memento, a remembrance. Whether it was her late husband's or her father's, I don't quite know, but as they said, that it was a remembrance and a memento, there was no need to go in to explain. The areas, the places where we come from, we all understand what we mean by a memento.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, did you ever go into a garage of any kind during these contacts you had?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, not at all. There was no garage at all. And I would call my kum into his apartment. He lived in the fourth floor in the other opposite building. He knows Hasan Oklopcic very well, and he had -- made jokes with him. And here in court, the court, he stated that he didn't know Hasan Oklopcic, and that is one of the gross lies that he said here. And the kum threw us the keys from his window. We switched the motor on. It was a blue Zastava-type car. Ms. Somers said Lada. It wasn't a Lada, it was a blue Zastava-type car. And the gentleman who testified a year ago and said the truth. And you will all hear the truth. It will come out. The truth will out and the truth has already come out in many press articles and books.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel make pauses between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Ms. Somers asked your wife something about this: What abuse was it to get a car out and go off with it? Can you explain this to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Alisic -- it was a white Golf car in Tukovi. I took the car and went to Alisic, Alisici. If you look at it from purely legal terms and rules and regulations, that might have been an abuse. But if you look at the end that was achieved through this little misdemeanour, then I don't take it to be any abuse. I saved a great deal of people from shelling in Alisici by using, borrowing the car, so I don't see that I had done anything wrong because the end was far greater. It is no abuse, to my way of thinking, because I helped a lot of people. But if you look at the strict rules of regulations where it says this, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Ms. Somers said that you used the car to take your wife's brothers, your brothers-in-law to Omarska and back.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: That is not an abuse. That all comes within the frameworks of the regular duties of a policeman. And I as somebody who had to -- who was issued fuel and everything I needed for the car and that I was issued these cars, I would always get one car, it would always be one vehicle, two vehicles at the most. And the individual -- anybody who has a positive -- that is to say, vehicles of this kind are issued to people who are fully responsible for their acts, because they have to account for the fuel used and everything else. And Mr. Zeljko told me that, without his knowledge, I should not give the keys to anybody else. Only he could say who was allowed to use the car because it was a requisitioned vehicle which might have been damaged and then the damage would have to be paid to the actual owner. So that is clear as day.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: What were your motives for going together with Mr. Gruban and his friend to the locality in question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: My basic motive -- I touched upon this a moment ago, but my main motive was that the end product of that affair was help and assistance. That is how I experienced it. And the gentleman, I don't know -- want to mention his name, and Gruban, I knew that they were friends of long-standing, that they were very good friends. Gruban would tell me that he visited him many times. He would visit him more often than he would come to visit me. And he asked me to come along because they'd feel more secure and safer. And knowing their relationship that was a proper friendly relationship, a trustworthy one, and that this would be a help to him, and as my wife insisted -- well, she didn't insist but it was her suggestion that I go and help them, all these circumstances led up to me accepting to help them, but only to help him. I wanted to help him, although nobody asked me for any similar help. They asked me for other types of assistance, but not that particular type.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: My last question for you, Mr. Kvocka: Did you personally take for yourself any single item of that jewelry, costume jewelry, or whatever you found?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: That is absolutely ludicrous. I don't know how to answer this. I maintain and claim and state, if you want to give me a death sentence, okay, but I say on pain of death that I never took anything or that I was offered anything. Nobody offered; I didn't take anything, nothing at all. It's an ordinary lie, a base lie which will come to the surface very soon, and we will hear publicly why that lie was stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers for the cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I want to try to reconcile two positions that have just been brought up. One is your wife's testimony that her motive for supposedly urging you to become involved in this was to help Gruban, and you just indicated that your motive, as encouraged by her, was to help AW because of his sick mother. Could you tell us which it is? Which is the real version of why you got involved? Your wife didn't mention a sick mother, and perhaps you could explain how this just surfaced.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, my wife and myself, we didn't have any talks as to how we would testify. She had her motives, which were hers; I had my own motives. But they were our motives. I don't know whether he mentioned his mother to her, except maybe after the first visit, but he did say that to Ckalja and to myself. I believe I addressed the issue of my relationship with Ckalja on several occasions and why I trusted him, why I asked him to watch over my brothers-in-law and some other people, so I don't want to go into that once again. But I can, of course. He was a well-respected man. He had many acquaintances, and people came to him for help. He was well disposed to that effect, and we have heard a number of testimonies as to Ckalja's character. I don't wish to repeat what they said about him. So there were some additional motives, if we can put it that way. My wife had an additional motive. For example, he used to bring apples from his village, the village of Maricka, to her brothers while he was on duty and I had already left. So maybe that motive was perhaps a stronger one for my wife. So it's difficult for me to answer why my wife had perhaps slightly different motives and why I had my motives.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You may not have talked to your wife just now, but at the time in 1993, did you talk to your wife about this? Did you share with her what you were about to embark upon?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, we agreed that it should be done. We had an agreement as to that, that we had to help him. Because you're trying to put it to me that we were about to loot some property. No. We wanted to help these people and you don't seem to be able to understand that. One can help people without asking for any compensation, without asking for anything in return.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, when you say, "We wanted to help him," "that we had to help him," whom? Help whom?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: That man, and also Ckalja. And because of this relationship that we had with Ckalja, it is my view that there was nothing fishy about it, that it was all very clear. I know what relationship they were -- that they had, Ckalja and that person, and I knew that Ckalja was on very good terms with this man and that this man was apparently going to leave him his apartment. So it was something that lasted for awhile. It didn't just happen out of the blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, on page 11942 of the transcript, Witness AW simply said, "I moved and became the komandir of the reserve police force of the police, and I was the komandir or leader for several municipalities of Prijedor," and went on to discuss regular training, and said, "But we were on duty with the regular police force every day." Where did you conclude that Witness AW held himself out as being a member of the regular police force? Where was that said?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: He stated clearly in his testimony - I may have received an erroneous interpretation, but that is what I heard - that he had been accepted in active service by his cousin. I didn't know that at the time, but I know that [redacted] was his cousin. And that he said he was a komandir at Urije. And then later on he changed it and he said that Zivko Knezevic -- I'm sorry, but I really have to give you my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, will you please slow down. You have raised an issue of misinterpretation, but if you continue speaking this fast, you won't receive an adequate interpretation. So please bear that in mind and slow down. Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I respectfully ask the Chamber to make an appropriate redaction from the record of the name that was given out that could lead to possible issues, that would conflict with protection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You're referring to page 54, line 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Witness AW went on, when asked, "How long did you work as a reserve police commander," a reserve police commander, on page 11943 of the transcript, "Until the beginning of the war in 1992." Again, I ask you: Where did you come up with your position that he was in the regular police force? Did someone tell you that other than officially?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, no. That is what I heard here from him, and that is why I started to laugh, because I think he was lying. He didn't want to look me in the eye and that is why I concluded that he was lying. A year ago, when I was answering your questions, I said that he was not for sure an active-duty policeman, and that is what I stand by. It was him who stated that he was -- that he became an active-duty serviceman, that he had left his job in the mining company. Those were his words; that's what he was saying here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Are you aware whether or not all of the people who were interned in camps, and in this instance Keraterm camp for this particular individual, if all of those persons nonetheless remained on the rosters of companies where they may have worked prior to their being detained? In your position at Omarska, would you have been able to learn that, dealing with thousands of detainees?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I will answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, what is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speculation, Your Honour. My learned colleague said, "in your position at Omarska." It is his position that is in dispute here and it will be decided upon by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, you should perhaps rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, based on your experiences during the war and perhaps in particular at Omarska, were the names of all the persons who had been detained in Omarska, for example, or perhaps other camps like Keraterm, were their names stricken from the rolls of their once employers; do you know that? Was there a need to do so?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know much about it. But in the interest of justice, I will tell you what I knew and what I heard and what I saw from the documents that you produced here. I know that in respect of certain individuals in respect of whom guilt was established or they were detained, I don't know how it was defined by the members of the Crisis Staff, decisions were brought to the effect that their employment had been terminated. I believe that you had a document to that effect which showed that some people had been discharged because they had been arrested pursuant to somebody's orders. I wasn't involved in that. I didn't have any commanding position. I was just a policeman who was on duty from time to time and I was not involved in that. My job was to provide security to those detainees and to prevent them from escaping. I actually told you about what my assignment was and what it included, but it only concerned me at my physical position and my post there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Following your logic, if persons had to be taken off of the rolls of their employers at the time they were detained, that would suggest, would it not, that they would have to be informed that they were detained, and that a record of detention would come from somewhere. Perhaps the camp itself. Are you suggesting that there was no coordination between the industries and those persons who ordered detention?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: I really don't understand why you need to make all these constructions --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Answer my question, please, Mr. Kvocka, and don't analyse my motives. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm trying to. You are interpreting and constructing things because you said that evidence was -- that there were registers to that effect. But there was nothing, there were no such logbooks in Omarska. There may have been people who sent such things, but we were not involved in that. We didn't have anything to do with such registers. We were just the police force providing security to the facility. That's, I believe, what was stated in that document and that's why I wanted to react. There was no evidence whatsoever that such records were kept, and that is the reason why I reacted the way I did, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, you said you spent some five hours digging for some 6.000 Deutschemarks. What was your position in the Prijedor police at the time of this event? Your exact position, your title, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: I wish I could remember exactly when it was, but it is quite probable that it was in the spring of 1993, as this gentleman stated. Maybe have even been in the fall of 1993. But nevertheless, I spent the whole year of 1993 working in Prijedor as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your position --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: In 1994 I became a shift leader - let me finish, please - and I was a police officer who worked on duty service for interventions. For brawls in cafes and things like that, I would be sent over to the scene to deal with that, together with another officer on duty, usually the driver. But I wasn't called upon, taking any serious measures, steps. You know what a police officer can do in order to prevent a fight.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: For at least five hours of a working day, you were away from whatever police duties you had. Did you explain to anyone above you what you were doing during those hours?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: It was during my free time. I didn't go there while I was on duty but when I was off duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You went past a checkpoint, according to Witness AW, and with a Serb signal to Serb officers at a checkpoint, you breezed through. Were you using your official position to breeze through a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, would you please ask your question in a direct manner. You're now making conclusions. Please go ahead and ask your question. You have the witness in front of you; you can go ahead and ask your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: What did you tell the Serb officers at the checkpoint, if anything, if you needed to tell them anything, about what you were doing going to a cleansed Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: We didn't have to submit any particular report. We just stopped for them to see me, and they knew me. It was just one of the checkpoints on the junction for Ljubija, and it was manned by the traffic police. In those days, there were no hostilities, there were no military activities, and there were no other such checkpoints. There was just this checkpoint with traffic policemen on it. They didn't ask me anything in particular because it was not forbidden for anyone to go there. And this three-finger salute that this gentleman mentioned - I knew you were about to ask the same question - is an absolute lie, a fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: How did you account for the other persons in the vehicle? If you got yourself through, was there any other issue about the other persons in the vehicle, Witness AW and Gruban?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, nobody asked anything. Gruban was wearing a uniform. They were colleagues so they probably -- that's why they didn't ask us for our IDs. They knew me and they knew him as well, probably. As I said, it was not forbidden to go there. One could go there. It's just that control was heightened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: You were wearing a uniform as well, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Correct, yes, except for the fact that we didn't have rifles, as this gentleman stated. We didn't have rifles because there were no rifles. Just a gun.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: When you returned and you came back from the village after you had removed the valuables -- excuse me, let me backtrack. When you came there again with a woman in the car, the relative of Witness AW --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't come back with a woman, no. It's a lie. Don't say that. His sister was not there. He said that she was in Tukovi, and he gave you a statement last year to the effect that she was in Raskovac. So there was a misunderstanding. They are two opposite parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Did you tell the persons at the checkpoint or any official, any official in charge of that area where you were digging, that you had removed property from that area? Did you tell them that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. There wasn't any official who was in charge for that area, neither did we have to submit any report. That was his property, so he didn't have to answer anything. But he was afraid because such were the times, and that's why he asked his friends, his acquaintances for help, people whom he could trust, and I believe that's quite clear to you as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... sister, was it not? It was not his property; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that. All I know was that he said that he would call his sister in [redacted] Whether she was in [redacted] or not, I don't know, but I hope that will become clear soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask for a redaction, please, of the record as to locations, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: There is no need. According to you, she was in Prijedor. So I don't see any problem with [redacted] now. Why would that be critical to you? Because according to her brother's words, she was in Prijedor in those days, but then [redacted] was mentioned. I don't see any reason why it should be stricken now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: And he called her on the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask for assistance, perhaps, in controlling the witness on this issue and a proper redaction. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpreters are complaining about the speed. We should have pauses between questions and answers. Yes, appropriate redactions will be made of the reference which was made about a country. Ms. Somers, will you please now try to finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I certainly will.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As a police officer, were you aware that there was a prohibition against looting or pillaging or removing the valuables of persons who had left the territory as a result of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: For me, as a policeman, ever since I donned my uniform in 1973, this prohibition against looting has always been applicable. That is a prohibition which is a permanent one, a standing prohibition, but this was not a case of looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, would it be correct to say that as long as Witness AW, and as he said, his sister, accompanied you, they would provide cover, an air of legitimacy for removal of goods from her own property; is that correct? They were your cover, were they not? They legitimised your action, didn't they? You did this in broad daylight with their cover.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: I really don't know what you're talking about. I don't know who protected whom. Are you trying to say that we protected them or it is them who protected us, as my wife said? I really don't understand what your objective is now, because we keep saying that we helped him, actually him and not them, because you keep putting in the sister who was not there. She was not present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Simic, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Just one question. Actually, several brief ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kvocka, Ms. Somers asked you about the fact that Witness AW was a member of the reserve police force. Did he mention that he was on sick leave and he was a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that prior to the war he was on sick leave and that after his sick leave he joined the active service, and that is what I heard. I don't know what is contained in the transcript, but I clearly remember what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did he say that he was admitted to the professional police station which was a completely different one from the one that he worked before?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. He referred to it as Prijedor II or Urije.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I think I know what you're going to say, but please do say it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The record speaks for itself. Mr. Simic is co-testifying with the witness about some explanation as to what he heard. It is inappropriate. The record speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept what my learned colleague has said, but I really couldn't keep silent, because apparently the witness was presented with a different portion of the transcript and not with the truth. We spoke about two segments of the problem here. The record speaks for itself, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course the record will speak for itself. However, Mr. Simic, if you closely look at the transcript, you will see that you have adopted a different position. You must not lead the witness in your examination. I have here only the English transcript which reads as follows: [In English] "... a police station which was a completely different one from the one that you were before." [Interpretation] Question should have been: "Did he tell you anything about so-and-so?" and then you continue with your question. You are fully aware of that, Mr. Simic, and the problem that I have is that as an intellectual, you are perfectly aware of the fact that you are leading your witness, and you know that you have other ways of asking your questions. Please do ask a direct question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: After his sick leave, Witness AW, did he work as an active-duty policeman at Police Station Urije II after 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's what he stated here, and I don't know whether it was true or not. He couldn't have worked there as an active policeman at Urije because I knew all other active-duty policemen, Popovic Milenko, Prodan Slobodan, Cvijo whom he mentioned, that is true, but he mentioned him because he was his neighbour. Cvijo Maric was his name. Zivko Knezevic, who was komandir at that time, and he said that he was actually the komandir.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: And my last question for you, Mr. Kvocka: My learned friend mentioned a document according to which the Crisis Staff stated that detained individuals could not be employed at the same time. When was the first time that you saw this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: When I came here in the detention centre and then later on again when the Prosecutor led that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: Later on you never saw such a document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Judge Fouad Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have just one question to clarify. You mentioned that the help you offered to Ckalja and his friend was the only kind of help which was asked from you or which you gave in that -- in this respect. Now, usually the help you gave was given to your in-laws, to your brothers-in-law, wasn't it? That was your main concern?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes and no. I helped many people in different ways, and many witnesses, even Prosecution witnesses, testified to that. I offered them protection and gave them assistance. Perhaps you didn't understand me. But when I said that kind of assistance, the kind of assistance was at their insistence. My wife and I decided to help them and do the job. Perhaps I didn't express myself properly, but that kind of help with respect to the digging up of this -- these things, that was the only time I did that, because of the overall relationships between me and Ckalja, Ckalja and my wife, and so on and the wartime circumstances. The other types of assistance, the other ways in which I helped people were not linked to this particular activity, because I helped my brothers-in-law, but I helped many other people as well. And as my mother said -- my wife said in 1992, 1993, the Muslims stuck to me like a stamp on a letter and then afterwards they ran away, but that is the expression my wife used, and I apologise for taking up this time to state that again. Now that we're home again, or she's home again, they're starting to stick to us again, asking for help. Some of them have apologised for testifying here. They didn't know they were testifying here against me. They ring my wife up from third countries and say they didn't do anything wrong. I don't know why. Something seems to have bothered them. Their conscience perhaps. But I'm not angry for any one of them for testifying here except this last person, because it was the first time that I heard such a flagrant lie in my life, not -- and in the Court here, not only in Court but in general. That was a flagrant lie. But I apologise for taking up your time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Kvocka, I have got several very specific, short questions. On these excursions, did you do the driving? Did you drive the car on these two days that you went? You did.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. And you, if I understand your testimony, or it may have been your wife's testimony, but one of you said that you were the one that asked for the loan of the car from Oklopcic; is that right? I don't know which one of you, but that either you or your wife asked to borrow a car from Oklopcic; right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, too, yes, because Oklopcic was a friend of ours from before, a comrade, and later we became kum, and we spoke about that relationship of ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Right. Right. I think you also testified that, under your version of what happened, this person whose name we don't mention, the friend of Ckalja's, that he also knew Oklopcic. Didn't you say that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Right. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: And I said that 100 per cent, because we joked with him when we asked him to throw us the keys out of his window. We were all present there when we took the car from him, and he threw the keys out of the window.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So my question is: In your impression, why do you think that Gruban or Ckalja felt he needed you to be involved at all if AW knew Oklopcic and -- I mean, what function did you perform in going along with them? Because as you pointed out, Gruban was also a policeman, had a uniform, and they recognised him at the Serb checkpoint. What function did you think you were performing? Why did they tell you they needed you to come?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, he -- a Muslim didn't approach another Muslim for help and assistance. It was a little tricky. And actually, a Muslim couldn't have helped another Muslim, so he didn't ask him. He asked directly, that is to say, Gruban's friend asked Gruban directly. And then Gruban said that they had to find a car, set about a time, that there should be a meeting point, that there -- where we should find a pick and shovel, and it's not easy to find picks. And I think Gruban, because the other man didn't know me, but it was Gruban's idea. And he told me later on when we stopped off for a cup of coffee, that is to say, after the first time, we had coffee and spent two hours drinking coffee and having a drink in my apartment, and he said that he had known about me, he knew everything about me, so he didn't appear to be afraid in any way. And so I think that Gruban suggested me, and he had nothing against him contacting me. So there was no special role, it was just better to have the two of us and him rather than having just the two of them. Gruban didn't have a car. He found it difficult to find a car. He didn't know people in Prijedor as well as I did. He couldn't borrow a care that easily. So they thought it was better to have two of us and one of him, the three of us rather than just the two of them. And the decision -- I apologise, Your Honour, but the decision because I myself thought that their relationships were quite clearcut and that there were no problems, that they were good friends and visited each other. Gruban visited him in his apartment nonstop. And after the events in Omarska, I would see Gruban in town and he would say that he was either on his way to visiting this friend or things like that. We always bring up the name of that friend of us and that's why I knew who he was, but I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You testified, I believe, that you went out on two separate days; is that right? You went out one day and then you went out sometime after. It's unclear as to whether it was -- one story is the next day, I think someone said -- no, it was a few days later. In between -- and did you use Oklopcic's car both times? On both occasions you used Mr. Oklopcic's car; right? Okay. In between, in between --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, both times I used Mr. Oklopcic's car. And many times during the war -- may I explain, Your Honour? I would like you to understand the circumstances that prevailed in our relationships. Many times, that is to say, Oklopcic wasn't a driver. His wife was a driver, and she had the car, the Zastava 101 car, registered in her name, and very often they would have a job to do and I drove Oklopcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Now, between the two trips, whatever time passed between the two trips, did you return the car, the car keys? You returned the car to Oklopcic after the first trip and then went -- then had to get the keys again on the second trip or did you just keep the car in between the two trips?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: I would give the keys back, and the car was usually parked in between the two buildings. So I saw -- I could see the car throughout the war out of my window. It was -- the two buildings were next to each other and I could see the car from my window. I could see his building and his car from my window. They were two apartment blocks, one next to the other, and the car would be parked there in between the two buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I believe your wife testified that there were some garages attached to the apartment complex, although you didn't have a car or didn't have a garage. I take it that Mr. Oklopcic did not park his car in the communal garage, or did he? You talked about it being parked between the buildings. It wasn't parked in the garage that was a part of the apartment complex; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's right. It was always parked in front of the building. And he would -- on both occasions he threw down the keys to us from the window. I don't know if he had a garage. Probably not, because he would have probably gone into his garage had he had a garage. At one point I would have seen it. But he never mentioned a garage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When you returned from both of the trips, you would take the -- you would park his car where -- did you park his car where he usually had it and then return the keys to him, and then the other people just went their way? Gruban, AW, they just went off by themselves or how did -- when you returned from the trip in both cases, just go through the movements in terms of your getting the car back.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: The first time when we got back and we didn't find anything, we parked the car closer to the entrance to my building, to my entrance, because we all went upstairs to my floor and apartment to have a cup of coffee and have a drink, an alcoholic beverage to get our circulation going, because it was night-time already. After that conversation and that time, they went off, and I went down and reparked the car, parked it closer to Hasan's apartment and took him back the keys. On the second occasion, the second time, his children -- his wife -- his son and daughter were playing in front of the building, so I gave them the keys. So the next time I parked directly in front of his building, and the first time I did as I have just explained it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My second question is: When you were out there at the site of the burned house, did you help with the digging at any point, or did you just watch while the other people were digging and trying to find the money or the valuables? Did you participate in the digging?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV KVOCKA [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did dig. Perhaps a little less than the other two, I didn't do as much digging as they did, because all this was a sort of strange atmosphere. But what can you do? That was what happened. But I did dig, yes. And after the first time, my wife washed my boots that belonged to the uniform and Ckalja's boots, she washed them for us. I remember that clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Mr. Kvocka, we have no more questions for you. We thank you once again for having testified, and I should like to ask the usher to ensure that you are escorted back to your place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours. And I apologise once again if I exploded several times, having been cautioned by you a few days ago, but this is the first time in my life that I have heard such a flagrant lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had four documents, if I remember correctly, which I would like to tender into evidence; two certifications on the non-possession of a garage and vehicle, and an excerpt from the personal file of Witness AW, and the request for departure from Prijedor municipality. So five documents in all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they are the documents that have already been marked, and they are D1/54 to D1/58 inclusive; is that right, Madam Registrar and Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Susan Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We have objections, Your Honour. If it's possible just to go through them chronologically and register our objections. As to the document labeled 1/54, which purports to be a document from the Ministry of Internal Affairs in Prijedor giving a negative indication of possession of a car, we think it is irrelevant. Possession, ownership/possession, we think it has no probative value in this particular line of testimony. There is no authentication of this document. It's a bit of a strange presentation. And the same person has signed off on two documents here that look as if they were prepared for litigation, frankly. I think both on issues of authenticity and on relevance, they would be inappropriate to admit. Now, the second document with the signature of a Nevenka Miskovic is D1/57, which purports to be a document from the Ministry of Internal Affairs concerning an address, the residence of Witness AW, and signing from this address for going -- purposes of going abroad. I think these documents are questionable. And 1/55A, there is no translation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting. Just one moment, Ms. Susan Somers. We're in public session. You have a document, the document is in the possession of a number of persons, and you are linking up the residence in the document and a witness. I don't think you're protecting the witness properly, or am I not seeing properly?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, I was trying to be as general as possible without -- just mentioning the pseudonym and then the nature of the document. There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But residence isn't a pseudonym. Residence is what it says. If I say to somebody that the name of a street and the door, and I state somebody's pseudonym, that could be served for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can identify the individual. I don't think I was translated properly. I apologise to the interpreters. Perhaps I was speaking a bit too fast, but I don't think what I said was translated properly. It's not important. But please proceed, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Can I just clear up the record, Your Honour, so that you're not under any misperception about what I asked. I did not mention any residence, any name of any residence. It was just the nature of the document. In case that was perhaps an interpreting problem, just so the Chamber is aware. I'm aware of the protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Susan Somers. I'm now going to speak slower in order to be interpreted. We have a document which has a number. The document is a public document. The document contains a residence which is concrete. So if you link up the residence in the document - the residence is a concrete residence - and the pseudonym of a witness, you run the risk of disclosing the identity. I don't know whether my idea has been properly transmitted. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. If there is in my -- if there was any possibility, even remote possibility, of making that link, it was unintentional. And if there is any redaction that would serve that - I perhaps didn't quite see it that way - but I would, in an abundance of caution, ask that we do review it and perhaps make appropriate redactions. In fact, if the Chamber is minded to admit any of these documents that have any possible connection, we would ask that they perhaps remain in confidential status, under seal, however the Chamber phrases it. Having reviewed two documents, 1/54 -- I'm sorry, D1/54A and D1/57, I'm moving on to D1/58. This purports to be something personal to the witness about whose testimony we discussed. There is no -- not even an indicium of authenticity, and I would indicate that it was prepared strictly for litigation. I think that it is inappropriate to consider for any purpose at all, based on what was given in evidence. Sorry, I must have missed 1/55. It is not translated, Your Honour. I'm just trying to take a quick glance to see. If we could defer this until there is a translation, it would be helpful. I don't necessarily see that this would be appropriate for admission, but I'd like to have the benefit of an official translation or even a draft. D1/56A and B purport to be registers or excerpts from the registers of real estate, and again prepared for litigation. It is unclear what the real records would reflect. And I think that this being a questionable summary of -- without any indication of why the original deeds or documents or any official document indicating the status of a piece of property was not produced, I think this is not an appropriate substitute and should not be admitted. It is a negative of something. Again, the term "possess," I don't know what they're -- if this is meaning ownership. And even if so, it is not evidence of the use of property at all. It really has no -- it's impossible to say what its value is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you finished, Ms. Susan Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Mr. Krstan Simic, let's hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I just agree with my colleague when she says that the documents have been prepared for litigation. But the preparation was such that we went to the competent institutions keeping these kinds of records and we asked them to look into their files and records and give us these certificates and data. The official institutions complied. It is a fact that we already said that within the Public Security Station, there is a public sector and that Nevenka Miskovic, the leader, was the head of this registration section, and that she issued two certificates with respect to ownership of cars, and that comes under her competence and jurisdiction. As regards the other two facts, it is stated in the heading that this is a record issued by the Land Surveying Institute and Service, and this is where the real estate records are kept, the real estate property of individuals. They are not found there as owners of real estate in Prijedor municipality. Had they established that they were owners of real estate, they would have issued a certificate to that effect. The institute of the iron ore mines looked at its own personnel files, and all this material is available to the Prosecution. It is true that the Trial Chamber will assess the probative value. Witness AW has lived for one and a half years in the opposite building. He said that Mr. Kvocka had a garage; we showed that he did not own a garage. The witness said he owned a car; we wished to prove that he did not own a car. The Trial Chamber will, of course, attach what weight it deems should be attached to these documents. But on the 9th of February, 1992, a contract, agreement, was made up on the utilisation of an apartment. We heard that he was thrown out. So documents of this kind do exist. The Prosecution could have come by these same documents and certificates. Let me say that the International Criminal Court is truly an institution which represents the community. All of us taking part in a procedure of this kind are duty-bound to act in this way vis-a-vis the witnesses we bring in, who come into this holy institution. That is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krstan Simic, thank you. There is, however -- you said a great many things, but there is a question that you have not responded to addressed by Ms. Susan Somers. She said that one of the documents was not translated, there wasn't a translated copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. K. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, there seems to be some confusion with respect to the distribution of the documents, because I, too, at the beginning did not have a translated copy. Now I do. Perhaps I have the copy that should have gone to Ms. Susan Somers. Could you clear that up, Madam Registrar, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. When I received the exhibits, they were not numbered and they were out of order, so I just distributed them. I probably inadvertently did not give Ms. Somers a copy, which I will supply to her after the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Having heard that, Ms. Susan Somers, we see that all the documents have their translations. I can confirm that. I have the translation of the document. Would you like to add anything, having heard that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would only ask to have the benefit of looking at the translated document and then reserving on it, if I could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We are now going to adjourn for lunch. Ms. Susan Somers can use the interim for looking at the documents. We shall be coming back and making a ruling on the decision, and to hear the other witnesses for the Prcac defence. A 50-minute lunch adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. Ms. Somers, have you now got all translations and does that change your position in any way?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I regret to inform the Chamber that the Registry was unable to provide a copy of the translation of 55 because it does not have the translation. It was not provided to the Registry. As to the other four documents, we remain -- we hold our position. This particular document has not been subject to our review for lack of translation. Our original, by the way, is with the -- the original in B/C/S is still with the Registry. I presume, Your Honour, that that means the Chamber also does not have an official translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, can you help us with this? Does that document have a translation or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, the problem is that we received a B/C/S copy and apparently an English copy was given -- it's the same English translation for two exhibits and that's the problem. I'm trying to work with Mr. Simic for getting the correct translation for D1/55. Also, when they're not numbered given to me, then it creates such a hassle, and I do request all that Defence counsel please number their exhibits before they hand them to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will, therefore, have to hold this decision in abeyance until further developments. Can I have my copy back, Madam Registrar, please. Very well. As we have indicated, the ruling will be postponed until this issue involving translation is clarified because I, too, am somewhat confused because it seems that one and the same translation has been submitted in respect of two documents. And since the documents were not tendered with numbers, it was impossible to identify the corresponding translation. We will have to wait, therefore. Mr. Jovan Simic, it is your turn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Defence calls Witness Petar Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic, I hope that you have in mind the decision of the Chamber. We will address the issue of the Omarska police department station and the incident involving gun dragging.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness is not going to talk about the incident involving the gun. He will only be speaking about the police station department in Omarska and the duties which were performed by the accused within that department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jokic. Can you hear me? Could you please come a little closer to the microphone so that the interpreters can hear you, and will you please now read the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for coming here. You will first answer questions that will be put to you by Mr. Jovan Simic. Mr. Jovan Simic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Would you please state your name, your surname, and your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: My name is Petar Jokic. I was born on the 21st of July, 1956, in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, that is, in May 1992, were you mobilised as a reserve police officer to the police station department in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could I please ask you to pause before giving me your answer, for the purposes of interpretation. Did you ever visit the investigation centre in Omarska while it was there, while it was functioning?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know the accused Dragoljub Prcac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Was Dragoljub Prcac also mobilised as a reserve police officer in the Omarska police station department?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was an active police officer or had he already retired?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: He was a reserve police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Drago Prcac was mobilised and where he was assigned to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: He was mobilised in May 1992, and he was assigned to the Omarska department.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of work he was involved with during that period of time while he worked there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: He worked as a crime technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did he work as a crime technician throughout that period of time in the Omarska police station department?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: In what period of time, that is, from what period of time was he no longer working in the Omarska police station department?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: From the month of July, but I don't know the exact date when he was transferred to the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you remember how it was? You said he went, he was transferred to the investigation centre. Did he come back after that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you situate us a little bit in terms of time framework? When did he leave, how much time did he spend there, when did he come back?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Two to three weeks. That is the period of time that he spent there and then he came back to the police station department.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: While he worked in the Omarska police station department, could you tell us who he worked with and what his working hours were?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: He worked with Rade Andzic who is also from Omarska. As to his working hours, I think it was non-stop or, rather, when necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: I think we will have to be a little more precise than that. Could you remember at least when it was that he came back to the police station department?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: June, July when he left over there, and he spent two or three weeks over there in the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: And you don't know when he came back?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: You don't know the month either?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I object. The witness has given a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness has already said that he doesn't remember the date. Mr. Simic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to get the month at least to find out at least what period of time it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, Mr. Simic. But he said it already, he said that he left at the end of June or July, that he spent two or three weeks there, and after that he came back. So the witness has already answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the detainees of the detention centre were transferred to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: You said you knew Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: While you were working with him at the Omarska Police Station Department, did you ever hear something about him receiving some money, or did you ever hear anything bad about him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, never. Nothing bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what your opinion of him is as a man.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: He's a very good person, a very good man. He's a good farmer. He has a family. He's retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Waidyaratne, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, could you tell us as to whether you were mobilised in 1992?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: In the Omarska department.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: As a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What was your duty?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: I was a guard there. I was providing security to the actual facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Could you be a little bit clearer, sir? When you say "I was providing security to the actual facility," what do you mean by "the actual facility"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: A guard, a watchman. I don't know how to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the actual facility"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: The station, that facility. That's what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, you are aware that the policemen from the Omarska Police Station were the people who provided security to the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: The reserve policemen and the active policemen from the Omarska Police Station were sent to the Omarska camp to provide security.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Prcac worked with Mr. Andzic. Could you kindly give us the first name, please?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Rade Andzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: He was also an active policeman, was he?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No. He was a reserve police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you didn't know when Mr. Prcac went out on assignments or his work as to what time he came to the police station and what he did during these assignments.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: I know that he came in late May, that he was a crime technician, that he would go out to visit the scene in cases of burglary or murder, up until the time he left for the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That's right, this is what you have heard. But you were not physically present with Mr. Prcac when he went to this place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness said that he knew, not that he had heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waidyaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I would move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: This is what you have heard from others, as to what you said about Mr. Prcac, is it -- is that your position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Jovan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I objected and my learned colleague was about to move on, but then he repeated the same question. The witness said that he knew, not that he had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: I would proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: How did you know, if I may put that question directly, how did you know as to what Mr. Prcac did during these assignments?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Because I was there. While I was on the same shift, he would tell us where he went and he would report back when he went out on the scene, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jokic, if you can be a little more clear. When Mr. Prcac came back, did he report to you as to what he did during his assignments and the places that he went? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: We knew in advance. When we had a report that somebody was supposed to go out to the scene, then the officers would inform us in advance where they were going before they would actually go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, my understanding is, correct me if I'm wrong, I thought you were providing security to the station. Did you have any role in what Mr. Prcac did?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you know that Mr. Prcac, during the time that he was attached to the Omarska Police Station, visited the Omarska camp on the orders of Mr. Meakic --

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, only when --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Please let me finish my question. On the orders of Mr. Meakic? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Meakic was the komandir of the department. He would come in, he would write down what our duties for the day were, he would come to see us, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, my question was: Did you know whether Mr. Prcac, during the time that he was attached to the police station, Omarska Police Station, visited the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: While he was there, that is, before he was transferred, no, he Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. didn't go; and afterwards, yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: What if Mr. Prcac, in his interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, has admitted that he had gone to the Omarska camp? If he has admitted that he has gone to the Omarska camp, what is your position?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: You will say that he has lied?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: So your position is that you don't know as to whether Mr. Prcac visited the Omarska camp during the time that he -- before he was -- when he was attached to the Omarska Police Station; is that your position? You didn't know.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAIDYARATNE
utterances.text: That concludes my questioning. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic, additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jokic, could you tell us whether, during the period of time you worked at the Omarska Police Station Department, were you ever on duty there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: You mean at the police station?

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the Police Station Department.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had our usual assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever inform Mr. Prcac about a theft or burglary or a murder or anything of that kind that happened there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Rade Andzic had a telephone. He didn't have a telephone, so he would call him because he lives close to his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand you. Did you inform --

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did inform Mr. Prcac about those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: Did you ever talk with Rade Andzic or Mr. Prcac about what happened after a particular investigation had taken place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would discuss those matters, of course. Thefts, burglaries, murders, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: So you had certain knowledge about those events and you would discuss them.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, we would normally talk about those events; of course we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: But you don't know whether he, formally speaking, ever compiled any reports. You don't know that. But you do have knowledge as to his presence and what he did there.

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. J. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Judge Fouad Riad, no questions? Madam Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, just one question. During the period of May, June, July, and August, while you were working in the Omarska Police Department, did you know of anybody besides Mr. Meakic, the commander, who worked part time at the police station and sometimes or part time at the Omarska prison camp? Did you know of anybody besides Mr. Meakic that did some work both at the site of the police station and at the site of the camp?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. For example, Borislav Bojic was at the police station. He was an active-duty policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And just to make sure I understand your answer, Mr. Bojic would work part of the time at the police station and some time at the camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No. No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me rephrase, let me repeat my question. I said during those months that we talked about, May, June, July, and August, did you know of anybody who worked some of the time at the police station where you were working and some of the time at the camp? The way you mentioned Mr. Meakic, who was the chief, would come into the police station, give orders, but he was also at the same time out at the camp some of the time. Did you know anyone else that worked in the police station part of the time and in the camp part of the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, let me make my -- I think I understand where we're getting confused. I don't mean that they worked, like, for a month in one place and then were transferred to the other but that they might work part of the day one place and part of the day the other or maybe a week or two one place and then a day or two the other place before they were formally transferred. Did you know anybody like that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Mr. Jokic, I have one question for you. If I understood correctly your testimony, you told us that Mr. Prcac came to the Police Station Department in Omarska at one point in time, then after awhile he left for the investigation centre in Omarska, and then finally came back to the Omarska Police Station Department. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did. Prcac came back when they were sent off to Manjaca. After that, he was taken back to the Police Station Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have also told us that he stayed at the investigation centre for two or three weeks, more or less?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, how much time did Mr. Prcac -- how long did he stay at the Omarska Police Station Department before he left for the investigation centre in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR JOKIC
utterances.text: How long did he stay there. For May until July. From the moment he was mobilised, up until June or July. I don't know. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Jokic, we have no other questions for you. Thank you very much for having come here. Let me ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovan Simic?
